prompt.context: Your client, Glycolia, is the manufacturer of mono-ethylene-glycol (MEG), a chemical which is mainly used in producing plastic bottles and antifreeze. Currently, MEG is produced using conventional sources through natural gas. Greenya, a research company, has recently registered a patent to manufacture environmentally friendly, green MEG using corn-based ethanol. Glycolia is thinking it may be able to charge a price premium for the green MEG and it is considering buying the patent from Greenya.
prompt.question: Should Glycolia buy the patent from Greenya?

clarifying_info.q: Is this patent unique in the market?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, this is the first of its kind. All current market players produce MEG using the conventional method.

clarifying_info.q: What is Glycolia's current market position?
clarifying_info.a: Glycolia is the second biggest player with 20% market share and annual sales of 1 million metric ton per year. The biggest player has 25% share and the third largest has 15%.
Glycolia sells its MEG to major consumer brands globally.

clarifying_info.q: Is Greenya open to other buyers?
clarifying_info.a: Greenya is interested in selling its patent to the highest bidder.

exhibits.title: Revenue — MEG Prices/MT
exhibits.shows: A bar chart showing historical and projected MEG market prices per metric ton from 2012 to 2016, growing at 2% annually.

exhibits.title: Costs — MEG Operating Costs/MT, 2016 (Projected)
exhibits.shows: A table comparing itemized operating costs per metric ton for conventional MEG vs green MEG production in 2016.

conventional_breakdown.depreciation: $40 (not labeled separately in exhibit — inferred from total; actually the listed items sum to ~755: raw materials 530 + labor 120 + utilities 45 + maintenance 40 + shipping 45 = 780; depreciation likely implied; use 755 as the conventional COGS per prompt)

framework: Revenue: additional revenue from pricing green MEG at a premium (20% above conventional), stronger PR and potential market share gains, by-products from the new production process, patent licensing revenue to other suppliers

Costs: Investment costs (patent acquisition price: $2B, plant construction and startup: $1B, total $3B upfront), operational costs (raw materials — corn-based ethanol vs natural gas, labor, utilities, maintenance, shipping, depreciation)

Risks: emergence of similar competing patents in the future, reverse engineering of the process by competitors, customers ultimately unwilling to pay the premium, single-customer concentration risk, regulatory or supply-chain risk for corn ethanol

questions.prompt: Prompt 2: Greenya is willing to sell the patent for $2B USD. Plant construction and all startup costs are expected to be $1B USD. Using the exhibits, conduct a DCF analysis to assess the feasibility of the green MEG plant as of 2016. Additional assumptions: prices and costs grow at 2% annually; green MEG priced at a 20% premium to conventional; plant commissioned in 2016; all construction costs depreciated over 20 years ($1B/20 = $50M/year, i.e. $50/MT at 1M MT/year); SG&A = $20/MT for both products; taxes = 30%; discount rate = 12%; use perpetuity formula for terminal value; ignore sunk costs (consulting fees of $50M are sunk).
questions.guidance: Candidate should build a per-MT income statement, convert to annual FCF, compute terminal value via growing perpetuity, then net against total investment. Key traps: (1) do NOT include the $50M consulting fee — it is a sunk cost; (2) DO add back depreciation ($50/MT) when computing FCF because it is a non-cash charge; (3) use the green COGS from Exhibit 2 ($930/MT), NOT the conventional COGS.

math.setup: Annual volume = 1M MT. Green MEG price 2016 = $1,000 * 1.20 = $1,200/MT. Green COGS (from Exhibit 2) = $930/MT. SG&A = $20/MT. Depreciation = $1B capex / 20 years = $50M/year = $50/MT (already included in Exhibit 2 green costs; confirm to avoid double-counting). Total investment (patent + plant) = $2B + $1B = $3B.
steps: EBIT per MT = Revenue - COGS - SG&A = 1,200 - 930 - 20 = 250 $/MT
FCF per MT = EBIT * (1 - tax rate) + Depreciation = 250 * (1 - 0.30) + 50 = 175 + 50 = 225 $/MT
Terminal Value (perpetuity with growth) = FCF / (discount rate - growth rate) = 225M / (12% - 2%) = 225M / 10% = $2.25B
NPV (2016) = PV of benefits - PV of costs = $2.25B - $3.0B = -$0.75B
math.answer: NPV = -$0.75 billion. The venture is financially unfeasible at the base-case 20% premium.

questions.prompt: Prompt 3: Drinkya, a major bottled beverage manufacturer and existing Glycolia customer, has offered an offtake agreement for 5 years in which Drinkya will buy ALL of Glycolia's green MEG at a 35% premium over conventional market price. Re-run the analysis. What should Glycolia do, and what strategic considerations should be kept in mind?
questions.guidance: Candidate should quickly re-compute FCF and NPV with the new 35% premium revenue assumption (holding costs constant). Then assess strategic pros and cons of a single-customer offtake agreement.

math.setup: Same cost base. New price = $1,000 * 1.35 = $1,350/MT. All other assumptions unchanged.
math.answer: NPV = +$0.3 billion. Financially feasible under the offtake scenario.

brainstorming.prompt: What strategic considerations should Glycolia keep in mind when evaluating the Drinkya offtake agreement and the broader green MEG opportunity?

categories.name: Pros of the offtake agreement
ideas: Demand certainty and stable revenue forecast over 5 years
Reduced shipping, overhead, and logistics costs from single large customer
Eliminates risk of unsold inventory and optimizes capacity utilization
Strengthens relationship with a major customer (Drinkya) and could lead to expanded partnership

categories.name: Cons / risks of the offtake agreement
ideas: Total dependence on one buyer creates non-diversification risk and exposure to Drinkya's own business cyclicality
Drinkya may renegotiate or walk away at contract expiry (after year 5), potentially seeking lower terms
Loss of pricing power once locked in; unable to sell to other customers at potentially higher prices
Reputational / operational risk if Drinkya encounters a crisis

categories.name: Broader strategic risks
ideas: Competitors could acquire a similar or superior patent in the future, eroding the first-mover advantage
The green MEG process could be reverse-engineered, nullifying the patent value
Customers may not sustain willingness to pay the premium long-term if environmental trends shift
Corn ethanol supply chain risk (crop prices, food-fuel competition, regulation) could spike raw material costs

categories.name: Alternative strategic options
ideas: Partner with Greenya (joint venture or licensing deal) rather than outright acquisition — lower upfront capital at risk
Buy the patent and license the technology to other MEG producers for royalty income — monetize IP without operating a plant
Explore PR and brand value from being the exclusive green MEG supplier to attract additional premium customers
Pursue volume growth by leveraging exclusive rights to gain market share and displace competitors

recommendation: At the base 20% customer WTP, the NPV is -$0.75B, making the outright patent purchase financially unfeasible and not recommended as structured.
Under the Drinkya 35% offtake scenario, NPV turns marginally positive (+$0.3B) on a $3B investment — the returns are thin relative to the capital at risk.

Recommend Glycolia NOT proceed with the full $3B purchase at this stage, but instead explore (a) a partnership or joint venture with Greenya to reduce upfront capital, or (b) acquiring and licensing the patent to other producers to generate royalties without full plant investment.
risks: A competitor acquiring this (or a similar) patent would erode Glycolia's existing market position and could render their conventional MEG capacity less competitive.
Corn ethanol input costs are volatile and could compress margins.
Single-customer dependency in the offtake scenario is a material concentration risk.
The 5-year offtake contract does not guarantee renewal on favorable terms, making long-term DCF assumptions uncertain.
next_steps: Negotiate with Greenya on alternative deal structures (JV, licensing, partial stake) to reduce the $3B capital commitment.
Conduct a competitive intelligence sweep to assess whether other MEG producers are approaching Greenya for the same patent.
Model scenarios where 2–3 customers (not just Drinkya) adopt green MEG at a 25–30% premium to test NPV sensitivity.
Assess the regulatory and supply-chain feasibility of scaling corn-ethanol-based production to 1M MT/year.
